content: The implications of any planned action, including legislation, policies, or programs, must consider the specific needs and experiences of women, men, girls, and boys at all levels. Gender mainstreaming is a critical component of the IA2030 vision, which aims to create a world where individuals of all ages, everywhere, can fully benefit from vaccines for improved health and well-being. The Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) evaluates the gender implications of its strategic and policy recommendations to promote gender equity. In alignment with IA2030 priorities, SAGE considers equitable vaccine coverage across genders, addresses barriers to immunization (including those related to caregivers and health workers), and promotes the full and equal participation of women in decision-making processes at all levels. At the global level, the World Health Organization (WHO) develops strategies to drive change at global, regional, and national levels. These strategies often address broader determinants of health and require cross-sectoral collaboration with various stakeholders, including social, economic, and political actors. While strategies are sometimes developed top-down, there is an increasing emphasis on involving strategic partners and stakeholders early in the process. The IA2030 strategy, for example, was developed through a collaborative bottom-up process, engaging thousands of stakeholders worldwide to reflect the needs of countries facing significant health inequities. This approach also incorporated lessons learned from previous initiatives, such as the Global Vaccine Action Plan and disease-specific efforts like polio and measles eradication. SAGE plays a key role in advising WHO on global health strategies, including identifying needs, gaps, and priorities; assessing feasibility and impact; and monitoring and evaluating progress. SAGE may also provide evidence-based policy recommendations and serve as an independent body to evaluate the outcomes of strategies. WHO vaccine position papers, which are based on SAGE recommendations, provide detailed guidance on the use of vaccines in large-scale immunization programs. These papers are intended for use by national public health officials and immunization program managers and are updated regularly to reflect new data or products. In situations of uncertainty or urgent need, WHO may issue rapid advice or emergency response guidance. This guidance is evidence-informed and transparently communicates any limitations or uncertainties. Such guidance is time-limited and subject to regular reassessment and updates as new evidence becomes available. These processes assess the quality, safety, efficacy, and programmatic suitability of vaccines. Manufacturers can apply for prequalification if their vaccines meet specific criteria, including compliance with regulatory standards and programmatic suitability. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems are essential for tracking vaccination coverage and assessing the impact of immunization policies. WHO and UNICEF jointly collect immunization data through the electronic Joint Reporting Form (eJRF), which helps identify trends and gaps at country, regional, and global levels. The IA2030 M&E framework includes tailored indicators to monitor progress toward immunization goals and strategic priorities, enabling continuous improvement of immunization programs. NRAs are responsible for regulatory oversight, testing, and release of vaccines, while WHO provides guidance on clinical development, trial design, and post-approval activities. WHO also supports the adaptation of global guidance to regional and national contexts, ensuring that immunization strategies address local epidemiology, resources, and priorities.
